opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think from the outside it looks obvious. You have this enormous pre-trained model that has absorbed a huge amount of knowledge, and you have reinforcement learning, which is how you get a system to actually pursue goals and improve from feedback. Put them together and you're done, right?

In practice it's much less obvious, for a few reasons. First, these two paradigms grew up in very different cultures. Pre-training is about scale, data pipelines, and predictable loss curves: you add compute, the loss goes down, and you can plan around that. RL has historically been finicky. It's sensitive to hyperparameters, reward design, and exploration, and it doesn't give you clean scaling curves. If you're running a lab and making multi-hundred-million-dollar bets, the thing with predictable returns wins the internal argument.

Second, the infrastructure is different. Pre-training is a big, mostly static batch job. RL needs a loop: you generate from the model, score those generations with some environment or verifier, and update. That means inference and training interleaved, often at very different throughputs, plus a lot of systems work to keep it from becoming the bottleneck. It's a different engineering stack, and that's a real cost.

Third, it wasn't clear where the reward would come from. RL is only as good as the signal you give it. For open-ended language, defining "good" is hard, and if your reward is a learned model, the policy will happily exploit it. It took a while for people to realize that domains with verifiable outcomes, like math, code, or anything with a checker, give you a reward that's hard to game. That's what made the combination start to really pay off.

And finally, there's a question of whether RL actually teaches the model new things or just sharpens what pre-training already put there. For a long time, a reasonable position was that it's mostly elicitation, so it's a nice finishing step but not where the capability comes from. I think that view is shifting as people push RL compute much further, but it's genuinely an open research question, and that uncertainty is part of why it wasn't treated as the obvious next move.

So I'd say it's obvious in hindsight, but at each point there were good reasons to be skeptical, and it took people stubbornly working on the unglamorous parts, like stability, infrastructure, and reward design, to make it look obvious.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s predictable loss scaling with RL’s sensitivity to hyperparameters, reward design, and exploration, identifying different optimization dynamics as a reason the combination was not straightforward.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training as a mostly static batch job and RL as an interleaved generation, scoring, and update loop, but does not clearly state that pre-training can use more compute in parallel per unit of elapsed time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually becoming obvious now, but it wasn't for a long time, and the reason is partly historical. Pre-training and reinforcement learning grew up as two very different communities with very different instincts. The pre-training world was about scale: you get as much data as you can, you make the model bigger, you make the batch bigger, and you measure loss going down. The RL world was about environments, rewards, exploration, and dealing with really noisy, high-variance signals. People in one camp didn't necessarily trust the other camp's tools.

And there were good reasons to be skeptical. RL has a reputation for being brittle. If you've trained a policy on Atari or on robotics, you know you can change a seed and get a totally different result. So when you've spent an enormous amount of compute on a pre-trained model that behaves nicely and predictably, the idea of handing it over to a process that's notoriously unstable feels risky. You're worried you'll destroy what you just paid for.

There's also a data question. Pre-training works because the internet gives you this almost unlimited supply of tokens for free. RL needs rewards, and rewards are expensive. Either you need a verifier, like math or code where you can check the answer, or you need humans in the loop, or you need a model that acts as a judge, and all of those have failure modes. So it wasn't clear that you could ever get enough signal from RL to matter compared to trillions of tokens of next-token prediction.

What changed, I think, is that the base models got good enough that they could actually explore meaningfully. If the model can't ever produce a correct solution to a hard problem, RL has nothing to reinforce. Once pre-training gets you to the point where the model sometimes gets it right, suddenly the reward signal is dense enough to learn from, and then you get this flywheel where RL teaches the model to reason longer and more reliably, and that compounds.

So in hindsight it looks obvious, but at the time there was a legitimate question of whether the two things would even work together, whether RL would just overfit to the reward and forget everything else. The fact that it works as well as it does is a little surprising, and I think we're still figuring out why.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s scale-and-loss objective with RL’s environment, reward, exploration, and high-variance signals, explaining that the two communities’ different approaches made combining them seem risky.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how much compute pre-training can use in parallel per unit of elapsed time compared with RL.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a natural thing to try, but it’s not obvious how to combine them well. In pre-training, you have a relatively straightforward objective: predict the next token over a large amount of data. With reinforcement learning, you need to decide what to reward, generate experience, and learn from that feedback. Those are different processes, with different costs and failure modes.

So the question is less, “Why wouldn’t you use both?” and more, “Where should you spend the next unit of compute?” Do you improve the underlying model, or do you give it more opportunities to practice and learn from outcomes? And if you run those processes together, does each actually make the other more effective? That’s something you have to establish experimentally.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s next-token prediction objective with reinforcement learning’s reward selection, experience generation, and feedback learning, showing why their optimization problems differ.

r002.rationale: It mentions different costs and how to allocate compute, but does not say that pre-training can use more compute in parallel per unit of elapsed time than reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it looks obvious in hindsight, but the two stages have very different properties. In pre-training, you have a relatively simple objective and a huge amount of data. With reinforcement learning, you have to decide what to reward, generate experience, and keep the optimization stable. Even knowing whether an improvement transfers beyond the tasks you’re rewarding is difficult.

So the question isn’t simply, “Why not combine them?” It’s where to combine them, how much compute to allocate to each, and whether the learning signals actually help one another. There are a lot of plausible approaches, and it isn’t obvious in advance which one will work.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s relatively simple objective and large dataset with reinforcement learning’s reward design, experience generation, and stability challenges, explaining why the stages are not straightforward to combine.

r002.rationale: It does not say that pre-training can use more compute in parallel per unit of elapsed time than reinforcement learning.
